title: How do AI devs handle level design?
author: Flaky_Opinion_829
selftext:
Hi there!  I don't have a strong understanding of how most AI-first devs leverage AI. I develop games as a hobby but I'm not an AI-first game dev (not fighting words), but my son wants to be a game developer when he grows up, so I want to learn more about this frontier. I would very much appreciate some insight in this domain.

I understand that many AI-first devs handle the programming and the art assets with LLMs, but assuming you were building something like Skyrim, what approach would some of you take to the level/world design?  Would you take the logic, assets, and world scaffold from AI and then build out caves, dungeons, and cities etc. in an editor like Unity's, or is the process purely iterative using agents and written feedback etc?

If it helps for context purposes, I've been a software dev for a long time and I do have experience with agentic development.

Thank you!

comments.author: count023
comments.body: Have the AI build a level designer tool and go nuts

replies.author: Nebuchadnezzar_z
replies.body: This is the way. Don't hardcode levels. Build a level generator. The algorithm is the juice.

replies.author: Glugamesh
replies.body:
People underestimate the power of being able to easily create tools to allow you to make assets. Need a level editor, make it. Need a voxel editor for specific assets, make it. Want a pixel art editor that works exactly the way you want and can output files exactly the way you need, make it. Need to make sound effects, make a generator. 

It's absolutely wonderful. I find myself having more fun making the tools sometimes.

replies.author: YoinkerDoinker
replies.body: Super baby level noob here, can I do this with a Unity project?

replies.author: count023
replies.body: aboslutely but not really necessary. the AI can create a level designer in something simple like hrml or javascript or whatever that will let you "svae" your levels into a unity scene structure, then yo ujust load that scene in as your level. Juist describe to the AI want you want in a plan, so stay if it's a first person shooter you'd want a "scene editor that allows you to place props (rocks, buildings, trees, vehicles...), characters (npcs, animals), and triggers (places where scripts or interactions might happen) and be able to be imported as a scene in unity. Tell it you need it to be easy to use like a webpage or walkable in 3d like you're in game, and then let the AI build it for you.

comments.author: counterclockwisdom
comments.body:
I am also interested in other people’s answers to this question. I haven’t tried AI for sketching out a phyiscal world area yet. I wonder if anyone can share their experience with this kind of workflow.

I figure it will be like generating art assets in that it can build out a lot quickly and can be guided by references and any clear rules you give it, but it will have terrible taste in actual level design, so deciding the central experiences and components of the level will have to be up to you (maybe with suggestions from AI, but not decisions). If your final goal is handcrafted-level quality, you will want to use a format that lets you most easily tweak the output yourself (edit / forgot to add: you may also be better off building the whole level yourself and improving your level design skill in the process. AI is that bad at it right now). Depending on what you’re doing, AI can probably help you make a decent level editor with specialized tools for making levels in your specific game.

replies.author: counterclockwisdom
replies.body: Wait, where did I describe procedural generation? I know AI can create textures and layouts/shapes very well through procedural tricks instead of assets, but as far as level design goes, my comment is about the designer or AI attempting to build with intention, which seems counter to random procedural generation of levels. What kind of procedural generation do you mean?

replies.author: joeyb908
replies.body:
"I figure it will be like generating art assets in that it can build out a lot quickly and can be guided by references and any clear rules you give it, but it will have terrible taste in actual level design, so deciding the central experiences and components of the level will have to be up to you (maybe with suggestions from AI, but not decisions)."

This is pretty much procedural generation via building blocks. Give it a few assets that are essentially Lego pieces (walls, floors, or specific voxel types tagged in specific ways), slap on a few layers of Perlin Noise, give it some rules, bounds, and limitations and you can basically create a main/alternate paths that it will generate around.

The actual level design and the main intractable gimmicks need to be hand-authored, but it's essentially a great way to get a large level made without having to hand-author the entire level. And with AI, it's easier than ever to make a very intricately detailed procedural set level generator/set dresser.

Look at games like Diablo and Path of Exile, tons of hand-crafted tilesets, but also massive backend of procedural generation to make endgame mapping not feel the exact same hundreds, if not thousands of hours in.

replies.author: counterclockwisdom
replies.body: I see. Using rules and authored components correctly, you can make a good random procedural level generator. That makes sense!

replies.author: MonkeyMcBandwagon
replies.body:
There are existing tools and methods that formalise the requirements of good level design into procedurally repeatable steps. 

For example a house layout designer has a set or rules, the (required) dining room and (optional) walk in pantry should both be adjacent to the (required) kitchen, some bedrooms lead to (optional) dead end bathrooms, at least one (required) bathroom must be accessible without traversing a bedroom etc. With enough of these rules working in conjunction, you can procedurally generate millions of houses that are at least always sensible, and often interesting and/or actually good.

I forget the exact name, but have read several devlogs around it, AI suggests it's called "graph grammars" but that doesnt sound right to me... it suggests the paper "Level Design as Model Transformation" as a good place to dive into that research.

Once you have a graph layout for the topmost layer, techniques like wave function collapse can fill in the finer details. 

All this to say, you could build a level designer, OR you could build a complex set of rules for procedural generation, OR you could build a procedural level rule definer to help build and modify that complex set of rules.

comments.author: QueenSavara

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: Build it manually, or procedurally genned. Most studios building open world games use some combination of the two (manual organization of points of interest + pcg (or whatever procedural system your engine or tooling supports) to cover in-between areas as well as strict rule hierarchies for painting textures, adding ground cover, etc.)

comments.author: LegendaryJohnny
comments.body:
I am creating RPG and it helps to have 10000s of hours invested into gaming.

But be careful with scale. Skyrim is extremely hard for 1 person if not impossible. When I started, my idea was to have locations from middle of Europe to Morroco in my RPG. Then I scale the idea down just to my country. Then I scaled it down just to my childhood city. And now I am thinking that maybe I wont make it from suburb of my city :D  

all in all I am happy so far how it is turning out, I basically created first map surface and level editor. Created first few buildings, I already know more or less the story for the area around first few buildings, then I created first few weapons for first levels, no need to go all in for end game weapon if you might never get to creating end of your game. then I created various RPG mechanics, looting system and raw combat. Then I spend dozens of hours fine tuning combat and adding more and more cool stuff to it - I am really proud now how it turned out - it is extremely satisfying turn based combat with good pacing and a lot of variety. Now I have everything and I am ready to create first questline in the first part of the map and I will go from there when finished.

comments.author: captfitz
comments.body:
AI is not very good at fully handling this part of game design yet. Designing big open maps requires too much intuitive understanding of hard-to-codify concepts like gameplay loops and progression. Maybe a future model will be good at it, but for now the most it can realistically do is build custom tools to help you design levels.

This is generally true across all aspects of game development. AI can execute really well, but it's not yet capable of making actual design decisions. You need to do the designing, AI will just help you make it real.

comments.author: Not-a-Clever-UN
comments.body:
Make sure to add "make no mistakes" to the prompt...

joking aside.  The industry term is whiteboxing a level.  The core parts of level design should basically look like building blocks.  A ramp here, a platform there, that kind of thing.  Once you have a whitebox, you could probably literally give an agent it and your art assets and say, "make this a village, keeping the overall feel of the whitebox"  or whatever it would be. 

Separately, I would ask your agent "what some good resources are for learning conceptual level design, with a preference for ones that mention working in agentic workflow and with some providence as a good resource."   Your "agent" can just be any of the free chat bot versions, or preferably several of the big ones looking for common answers, since this is a simple resource search.  

Even if you do procgen type stuff, like you might for "dungeon rooms" you'd still likely want to whitebox each room.  For example, Gunfire Reborn uses procgen tiled rooms, but each one was handmade so there's good cover positions, good ambush positions, etc.   For "skyrim" you'd want a place that's good for ranged attacks, a place that's good for a melee attack, possibly locations where a trap could appear, etc.

comments.author: Fancy-Proof-9449
comments.body:
For my game the mazes are generated, not hand made, and the AI wrote the generator. What made that work was not the generator, it was the test around it. Every build runs the maze generator on 40 seeds and checks that every one is fully connected and that the same seed always gives the same maze. If a change breaks that, the build fails before I ever see it.

Without that check I would have been playing hundreds of mazes by hand looking for the one that traps you. With it I only play to judge whether it feels good, which is the part the AI can't do.

So my answer is close to what others said: let the AI build the tool, but also have it write the checks that prove the tool's output is legal. Then your time goes into taste, like where the big rooms go and what the player sees first, not into finding broken levels.

comments.body: I brought an AI into an existing game, had it read the memory so it could see positioning and take screenshots to learn how to use props creatively and also taught it some design principles. I use it for level design and also to decorate points of interest
